issues.legal_issue: A sonless Jain widow may adopt a son to her deceased husband without his express authority where the general Jain custom permitting such adoption applies.
material_facts: A widow from a Jain community adopted a son to her deceased husband without express authority from him.
The adoption was challenged because no custom specific to the widow’s sect and locality had been proved.
Judicial decisions over a long period had recognized the custom among Jains generally outside the Madras and Punjab areas, without limiting it to particular Jain sects.
issues.conclusion: The adoption was valid because the generally recognized Jain custom applied, notwithstanding the absence of proof of a custom specific to the parties’ sect or locality.
issues.legal_principle: Jains generally follow Hindu law in the absence of a contrary usage. A custom repeatedly recognized by courts may become part of the law applicable to the community and need not be proved afresh in every case. The court relied particularly on Pemraj v. Mst. Chand Kanwar and Mangibai Gulabchand v. Suganchand Bhikamchand, and referred to Rama Rao v. Raja of Pittapur on judicial recognition of custom; it distinguished the general application of an established custom from an unsupported deduction of one custom from another, as discussed in Saraswathi Ammal v. Jagadambal.

rule.if: jain_adoption_dispute and widow_adopted_for_deceased_husband and husband_gave_no_express_authority and general_jain_custom_was_judicially_established and community_outside_custom_exceptions

predicates.jain_adoption_dispute: The proceeding concerns the validity of an adoption in a Jain community.
predicates.widow_adopted_for_deceased_husband: A widow adopted a son to her deceased husband.
predicates.husband_gave_no_express_authority: The deceased husband had not expressly authorized the adoption.
predicates.general_jain_custom_was_judicially_estab: Courts had repeatedly recognized a general custom among Jains permitting a widow to adopt without her deceased husband’s authority.
predicates.community_outside_custom_exceptions: The community was outside the areas in which the recognized general custom did not apply.

issues.definition: When a Jain adoption dispute involves a widow who adopted for her deceased husband without his express authority, the generally established custom applies outside its recognized exceptions and the adoption is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A female holder’s share declared by a preliminary partition decree is possessed property that becomes her absolute property when the applicable succession regime is in force at her death, even if the share has not been physically divided.
material_facts: A preliminary decree in a partition suit declared a female family member entitled to a share in joint family property.
The property remained with the family and in joint enjoyment; the share had not been physically separated before her death.
She died after the Hindu Succession Act had come into force, and the dispute concerned who inherited her share.
The court held that the share devolved under the statutory succession rules on the female holder’s heirs in the preferred class, excluding a more remote claimant.
issues.conclusion: The declared share was possessed by the female holder and became her absolute property; on her intestate death it devolved under the applicable succession rules on the heirs in the preferred class.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14, 15 and 16 of the Hindu Succession Act apply to Jains through section 2(1)(b). Section 14 gives a female Hindu full ownership of property possessed by her, and “possessed” bears the broad meaning of owning or having property in one’s power. The court relied on Gumalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veerayya for that meaning. It held that section 4 supersedes inconsistent prior Hindu-law rules where the Act makes provision, and that the rule in Pratapmull Agarwalla v. Dhanabati Bibi—that a share declared for a wife or mother is not owned until actual division—does not govern after the Act. Sections 15 and 16 determine the order and manner of succession.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and preliminary_decree_declared_female_share and share_remained_in_joint_possession and female_holder_died_intestate_after_succession_reform_took_effect

predicates.partition_proceeding: The case concerns the division of family property in a partition proceeding.
predicates.preliminary_decree_declared_female_share: A preliminary decree declared a female family member entitled to a share of the property.
predicates.share_remained_in_joint_possession: The declared share had not been physically separated and remained in the family’s joint possession or enjoyment.
predicates.female_holder_died_intestate_after_succe: The female holder died without a will after the applicable succession reform had taken effect.

issues.definition: If a partition decree declares a female holder’s share, the share remains in joint possession, and she dies intestate after the succession reform takes effect, the share is her absolute property and devolves under intestate succession.

issues.legal_issue: Authorizing a commissioner to investigate property and liabilities and propose a partition does not abdicate the court’s judicial function when the court retains the task of hearing and deciding the proposals.
material_facts: In a partition suit, the trial court authorized a commissioner to ascertain the property and family liabilities and to submit proposals for partition.
The commissioner could gather information and record evidence as necessary, but the proposals were not binding on the parties.
The court retained the authority to hear the parties and adjudicate the proposals.
The order had been made with the parties’ consent, and no objection to it had been pressed before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The commissioner’s appointment did not amount to an abdication of the court’s functions, and no modification of the decree was warranted on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A court does not delegate its judicial function merely by directing a commissioner to investigate matters and submit non-binding proposals, where the court itself retains the power to hear the parties and decide the issues. The court relied on the nature and limits of the commissioner’s assignment and the court’s retained adjudicative role.

predicates.appeal_from_partition_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree in a partition case.
predicates.commissioner_was_directed_to_prepare_non: A commissioner was asked to investigate relevant matters and submit proposals that did not bind the parties.
predicates.court_retained_power_to_hear_and_decide: The court retained authority to hear the parties and make the final decision.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a partition decree, a commissioner’s assignment to prepare non-binding proposals does not abdicate judicial functions if the court retains the power to hear and decide.
